pos: n. (the chest; in the law, the wave-offering portion; rendering Hebrew chazeh, shad, Greek stethos)
etymology: From Anglo-Saxon breost. In the Levitical law the breast is a technical term — the portion of the peace offering waved before the LORD and then given to the priests.
biblical_def: Breast in the Authorized Version is most often a sanctuary word. In the peace offering the fat was burned to God and “the breast shall be Aaron's and his sons'” (Lev 7:31) — waved before the LORD first, then eaten by the priests, so that the same portion was both given to God and received from Him. Moses took the breast of the ram of consecration and waved it as his own part (Lev 8:29). The arrangement is stated as a perpetual statute: “the wave breast and the heave shoulder have I taken of the children of Israel… and have given them unto Aaron the priest” (Lev 7:34), and the priests were to eat it “in a clean place” (Lev 10:14). The breast is therefore a standing picture of ministerial support: those who serve at the altar live of the altar, and what they eat has passed through God's hands first. It is never simply a wage; it is a portion waved.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the breast as the soft protuberant body adhering to the thorax, and by extension the seat of the affections and passions — whence to lay to heart, and to trust in one's own breast.
webster_full: BREAST, n. The soft, protuberant body, adhering to the thorax, which, in females, furnishes milk for infants.
2. The fore part of the thorax, or the fore part of the human body between the neck and the belly.
3. Figuratively, the heart; the conscience; the disposition; the affections.
4. The breast of a beast, as a portion in sacrifice, was given to the priest.
scriptures: Lev 7:31
And the priest shall burn the fat upon the altar: but the breast shall be Aaron's and his sons'.
Lev 7:34

For the wave breast and the heave shoulder have I taken of the children of Israel from off the sacrifices of their peace offerings, and have given them unto Aaron the priest and unto his sons by a statute for ever from among the children of Israel.
Lev 8:29
And Moses took the breast, and waved it for a wave offering before the LORD: for of the ram of consecration it was Moses' part; as the LORD commanded Moses.

And the wave breast and heave shoulder shall ye eat in a clean place; thou, and thy sons, and thy daughters with thee: for they be thy due, and thy sons' due, which are given out of the sacrifices of peace offerings of the children of Israel.
corruption_summary: A body that Scripture treats as an offering reduced to an object of appetite or a matter of shame — and, on the ministerial side, a portion waved before God turned into a mere salary negotiation.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the shape of the wave offering itself. The breast was lifted toward God before it ever reached the priest's table, and that order is the whole doctrine of ministerial support. A congregation that pays its elders as employees, and elders who receive it as earnings, have both lost the wave. What sustains a minister is first given to God and then given back, which is why 1 Corinthians 9 can insist on the right and Paul can decline to use it without contradiction.

The second recovery concerns the body. Scripture speaks of the breast plainly, without either the leer or the flinch that modern culture alternates between — as the nursing mother's provision, as the seat of the affections, and as a portion holy to the LORD. That God should claim a portion of a sacrificed body and call it holy is a rebuke to every account of the body as merely biological, and to every account that treats it as shameful.
roots_summary: Hebrew chazeh (H2373), the breast of a sacrificial animal, the wave portion; shad (H7699), the breast that nurses; Greek stethos (G4738), the chest — where John leaned at the supper.
roots_lines: Hebrew chazeh (H2373) — the breast of the offering, waved before the LORD and given to the priests (Lev 7:34).
Hebrew tenuphah (H8573) — a waving, the wave offering; the motion that made the portion holy before it was eaten.
Greek stethos (G4738) — the breast, chest; the publican smote upon his breast (Luk 18:13), and the disciple leaned on Jesus' breast.
usage: “The breast shall be Aaron's and his sons'” — the priests' portion of the peace offering.
“The wave breast and the heave shoulder have I taken… and have given” — taken by God, then given.
“Shall ye eat in a clean place” — even the minister's bread is a holy thing.

pos: n. (the height of the body; figuratively, maturity; rendering Hebrew qomah, middah, Greek helikia)
etymology: From Latin statura, from stare, to stand — how tall a man stands. Scripture repeatedly refuses to let the measurement settle anything.
biblical_def: Stature is height, and Scripture uses it chiefly to overturn the judgment men make from it. The spies were undone by it — “all the people that we saw in it are men of a great stature” (Num 13:32) — and their report is called evil. The correction comes at the anointing of David: “Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature; because I have refused him: for the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart” (1Sa 16:7). Isaiah promises the whole class of the tall will be felled: “the high ones of stature shall be hewn down, and the haughty shall be humbled” (Isa 10:33). The Lord Jesus then makes stature the proof of anxiety's futility — no man by taking thought can add a cubit to it (Mat 6:27) — and Scripture reassigns the word to what actually matters: Christ “increased in wisdom and stature” (Luk 2:52), and the church grows “unto the measure of the stature of the fulness of Christ” (Eph 4:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines stature as the natural height of an animal body, chiefly used of man — and notes that it is applied to the height of a person considered as an indication of dignity or strength.
webster_full: STAT´URE, n. The natural highth of an animal body. It is more generally applied to the human body.
Foreign of stature, and of beauty rare.
Which of you by taking thought can add one cubit unto his stature? Matt. vi.
scriptures: But the LORD said unto Samuel, Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature; because I have refused him: for the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart.
Mat 6:27
Which of you by taking thought can add one cubit unto his stature?
Eph 4:13
Till we all come in the unity of the faith, and of the knowledge of the Son of God, unto a perfect man, unto the measure of the stature of the fulness of Christ:

And they brought up an evil report of the land which they had searched unto the children of Israel, saying, The land, through which we have gone to search it, is a land that eateth up the inhabitants thereof; and all the people that we saw in it are men of a great stature.
corruption_summary: The eye's verdict trusted absolutely — appearance as credential in pulpit, politics, and platform — which is precisely the judgment 1 Samuel 16:7 was written to overturn.
corruption_paragraphs: An image-saturated culture has made outward appearance a nearly irresistible qualification. Height, beauty, and presence still select leaders, and the church is not exempt: pulpits are filled by charisma and platforms by photogenic confidence, while 1 Samuel 16:7 is quoted in devotionals and ignored in decisions. The verse is not sentimental. It records God refusing a candidate Samuel had already approved on sight, and the man Samuel approved was tall.

The remedy is not indifference to the body, which Scripture never counsels, but the reassignment of the word. Ephesians 4:13 gives the church a growth chart with only one mark on it — the stature of the fulness of Christ — and Luke 2:52 shows the Lord Jesus growing in both senses at once. Meanwhile Matthew 6:27 quietly removes the anxiety that drives the whole business: no amount of thought adds a cubit. What a man cannot alter he is not required to justify.
roots_summary: Hebrew qomah (H6967), height, from qum, to rise; middah (H4060), measure; Greek helikia (G2244), stature and also age or maturity — both senses live in Eph 4:13.
roots_lines: Hebrew qomah (H6967) — height, stature; the great stature of the Anakim (Num 13:32) and the high ones hewn down (Isa 10:33).
Greek helikia (G2244) — stature, and also age or maturity; the double sense is deliberate in Luk 2:52 and Eph 4:13.
Hebrew lebab (H3824) — the heart; what the LORD looks upon instead of the height (1Sa 16:7).
usage: “Man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart” — a candidate refused on sight.
“Which of you by taking thought can add one cubit unto his stature?” — anxiety's futility.
“Unto the measure of the stature of the fulness of Christ” — the church's only growth chart.

pos: n. (a stroke of a whip, and the weal it leaves; rendering Hebrew chabburah, Greek molops, plege)
etymology: From Middle Dutch strijpe, a streak — the mark left on the skin, not merely the blow. Isaiah 53 turns on the fact that the word means a visible wound.
biblical_def: Stripe is the lash and the mark it leaves, and Scripture governs it with a mercy unknown in the ancient world. Forty stripes is the ceiling, and the reason given is startling: “lest, if he should exceed… then thy brother should seem vile unto thee” (Deu 25:3). The limit protects the offender's dignity, not merely his back; he is still a brother when the beating ends. Proverbs measures the difference between men by how few strokes they need: “A reproof entereth more into a wise man than an hundred stripes into a fool” (Pro 17:10). The Lord Jesus makes stripes proportional to knowledge — many for the servant who knew his lord's will, few for the one who did not (Luk 12:47) — which is the plainest statement in Scripture that judgment is graded. And all of it converges on Isaiah: “he was wounded for our transgressions… and with his stripes we are healed” (Isa 53:5), the marks on His back becoming the medicine for ours.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a stripe as a stroke made with a lash, whip or rod, and also the weal or long narrow mark discolored by such a stroke — and secondarily a line or band of colour.
webster_full: STRIPE, n. A line or long narrow division of any thing, of a different color from the ground.
2. A stroke made with a lash, whip, rod, strap or scourge; also, the weal or long narrow mark discolored by such a stroke.
Forty stripes he may give him and not exceed. Deut. xxv.
3. Figuratively, affliction; punishment; sufferings.
scriptures: Isa 53:5
But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.
Deu 25:3
Forty stripes he may give him, and not exceed: lest, if he should exceed, and beat him above these with many stripes, then thy brother should seem vile unto thee.
A reproof entereth more into a wise man than an hundred stripes into a fool.
And that servant, which knew his lord's will, and prepared not himself, neither did according to his will, shall be beaten with many stripes.
corruption_summary: Isaiah 53:5 detached from its context and turned into a guarantee of bodily healing on demand — a reading that ignores the verse's own subject, transgressions and iniquities.
corruption_paragraphs: “With his stripes we are healed” is among the most misused sentences in the Bible. The healing-on-demand teaching lifts the clause out of a verse that has already named the disease twice — He was wounded for our transgressions, bruised for our iniquities — and Peter, quoting it, states the purpose without ambiguity: that we, being dead to sins, should live unto righteousness (1Pe 2:24). The healing in view is the healing of sinners. Bodily healing is a real mercy and a real promise, and its full payment is the resurrection, not this afternoon.

Deuteronomy 25:3 deserves its own recovery, because it is one of the most humane sentences in ancient law. The limit is set so that thy brother should seem vile unto thee — excessive punishment degrades the punisher's view of the punished, and the law forecloses it. Every doctrine of discipline, in home or church, is bound by that principle: correction that destroys a man's standing as a brother has exceeded its warrant, however deserved the first stroke was.
roots_summary: Hebrew chabburah (H2250), a weal, bruise, the mark of a blow — the word of Isa 53:5; Greek molops (G3468), a bruise or welt, used by Peter; plege (G4127), a stroke or plague.
roots_lines: Hebrew chabburah (H2250) — a stripe, weal, bruise; with his stripes we are healed (Isa 53:5), the visible mark rather than the blow.
Greek molops (G3468) — a bruise, welt; Peter's rendering of Isaiah, tied explicitly to dying to sins (1Pe 2:24).
Greek plege (G4127) — a stroke, wound, plague; the many and few stripes of Luk 12:47-48, graded by knowledge.
usage: “With his stripes we are healed” — and the verse names the disease: transgressions and iniquities.
“Forty stripes he may give him, and not exceed” — the limit guards the offender's dignity.
“Shall be beaten with many stripes… with few stripes” — judgment is graded by knowledge.

pos: adj. (unable or unwilling to speak; rendering Hebrew illem, damam, Greek kophos, alalos)
etymology: From Anglo-Saxon dumb, mute. The Authorized Version never uses it to mean stupid; it means speechless, whether by affliction, by choice, or by judgment.
biblical_def: Dumb means without speech, and Scripture uses it in four ways. It is an affliction God claims sovereignty over: “Who hath made man's mouth? or who maketh the dumb, or deaf…? have not I the LORD?” (Exo 4:11) — spoken to Moses, who was pleading a speech impediment as a disqualification. It is a chosen silence under God's hand: “I was dumb, I opened not my mouth; because thou didst it” (Psa 39:9). It is a judgment on unfaithful ministers — Isaiah's watchmen are “dumb dogs, they cannot bark” (Isa 56:10), the most damning phrase in Scripture for a preacher who will not warn. And supremely, it is the willing silence of the Substitute: “as a sheep before her shearers is dumb, so he openeth not his mouth” (Isa 53:7). Against all of it stands the command that the church has no excuse to ignore: “Open thy mouth for the dumb” (Pro 31:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines dumb as mute, silent, not speaking — and as destitute of the power of speech, as a dumb beast, noting that it does not signify want of understanding.
webster_full: DUMB, a. Mute; silent; not speaking.
I was dumb with silence, I held my peace. Ps. xxxix.
2. Destitute of the power of speech; unable to utter articulate sounds; as the dumb brute.
3. Not accompanied with speech; as a dumb show.
scriptures: Exo 4:11
And the LORD said unto him, Who hath made man's mouth? or who maketh the dumb, or deaf, or the seeing, or the blind? have not I the LORD?
Isa 53:7
He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth: he is brought as a lamb to the slaughter, and as a sheep before her shearers is dumb, so he openeth not his mouth.
Pro 31:8
Open thy mouth for the dumb in the cause of all such as are appointed to destruction.
His watchmen are blind: they are all ignorant, they are all dumb dogs, they cannot bark; sleeping, lying down, loving to slumber.
corruption_summary: The pulpit made dumb by prudence — silence on whatever costs a hearing, rebranded as winsomeness — while Proverbs 31:8 commands the opposite use of the mouth.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 56:10 is a permanent indictment of ministerial silence, and the image is exact: a watchdog that will not bark is worse than useless, because his presence persuades the household it is guarded. A ministry that avoids every subject on which its people are actually being deceived has become a dumb dog, whatever its attendance. And the modern euphemisms for it — being winsome, keeping the main thing the main thing, not being political — are precisely the vocabulary Isaiah's watchmen would have used.

The counterpoise is that Scripture also commends silence, and the church must know which is which. Psalm 39:9 is a saint choosing not to speak because thou didst it — silence under providence, not before error. And Isaiah 53:7 shows the Lamb dumb before His accusers, which is the pattern for suffering wrongfully rather than for teaching. The rule that sorts them is Proverbs 31:8: open thy mouth for the dumb. Speech is owed to those who cannot speak for themselves; silence is permitted about oneself.
roots_summary: Hebrew illem (H483), mute, speechless; damam (H1826), to be still, silent; Greek kophos (G2974), blunted in speech or hearing; alalos (G216), without speech.
roots_lines: Hebrew illem (H483) — dumb, unable to speak; the dumb whose cause Pro 31:8 commands the king to plead, and the dumb sheep of Isa 53:7.
Hebrew damam (H1826) — to be silent, still; the psalmist's chosen dumbness under God's hand (Psa 39:9).
Greek kophos (G2974) — blunt, dull; used of both deafness and dumbness, since the two afflictions travel together (Mar 7:37).
usage: “Who maketh the dumb, or deaf…? have not I the LORD?” — sovereignty claimed over affliction.
“They are all dumb dogs, they cannot bark” — the indictment of a silent ministry.
“Open thy mouth for the dumb” — speech owed to those who have none.

pos: adj. (unable or unwilling to hear; rendering Hebrew cheresh, Greek kophos)
etymology: From Anglo-Saxon deaf. Because in Hebrew hearing and obeying are one word, deafness becomes Scripture's natural figure for a will that will not submit.
biblical_def: Deaf in Scripture is both a bodily affliction and a spiritual condition, and the two are held together deliberately. The law protects the deaf man with a striking motive: “Thou shalt not curse the deaf, nor put a stumblingblock before the blind, but shalt fear thy God” (Lev 19:14) — the offence is possible precisely because the victim cannot detect it, so the restraint must come from the fear of God alone. That verse governs every cruelty done behind a back. God claims the making of the deaf as His own work (Exo 4:11). Isaiah then turns the word on the covenant people: “Who is blind, but my servant? or deaf, as my messenger that I sent?” (Isa 42:19) — the worst deafness belongs to those charged with hearing. And the messianic promise is stated in the same terms: “the ears of the deaf shall be unstopped” (Isa 35:5), fulfilled in the ministry the crowds summarized so well — “he maketh both the deaf to hear, and the dumb to speak” (Mar 7:37).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines deaf as not perceiving sounds, wanting the sense of hearing, and figuratively as inattentive, not listening, refusing to hear or to regard.
webster_full: DEAF, a. Not perceiving sounds; not receiving impressions from sonorous bodies through the air; as a deaf ear.
2. Wanting the sense of hearing; having organs which do not perceive sounds; as a deaf man.
3. Not listening or regarding; not moved, persuaded or convinced; rejecting; as, deaf to reason or arguments.
4. Deprived of the power of hearing; deafened; as deaf with clamor.
scriptures: Thou shalt not curse the deaf, nor put a stumblingblock before the blind, but shalt fear thy God: I am the LORD.
Isa 35:5
Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall be unstopped.
Who is blind, but my servant? or deaf, as my messenger that I sent? who is blind as he that is perfect, and blind as the LORD'S servant?
Mar 7:37
And were beyond measure astonished, saying, He hath done all things well: he maketh both the deaf to hear, and the dumb to speak.
corruption_summary: Deafness of the will excused as honest doubt — and, in practice, the church's failure to keep Leviticus 19:14, where cruelty is restrained only by the fear of God.
corruption_paragraphs: Leviticus 19:14 anticipates the exact form most cruelty takes: harm done where the victim cannot perceive it. Cursing a deaf man costs nothing socially, since he will never know; tripping a blind man can always be denied. The law offers no external enforcement and appeals instead to a single restraint — but shalt fear thy God. That is the standing answer to gossip, to the anonymous word, and to every unkindness performed at a safe distance.

The spiritual sense is where the age evades. Refusal to hear is now regularly presented as intellectual honesty, and Isaiah 42:19 aims the charge at exactly the people most confident of hearing: Who is deaf, as my messenger that I sent? Yet the entry cannot end there, because the promise outruns the diagnosis. The ears of the deaf shall be unstopped, and Mark 7:37 records it done. The One who claims in Exodus 4:11 to make the deaf is the One who opens them.
roots_summary: Hebrew cheresh (H2795), deaf, from a root meaning to be silent or dull; Greek kophos (G2974), blunted — used of ears and tongue alike; the opposite of shama, to hear and obey.
roots_lines: Hebrew cheresh (H2795) — deaf; protected by law (Lev 19:14) and healed by promise (Isa 35:5).
Hebrew shama (H8085) — to hear, and thereby obey; deafness is its exact negation, which is why the figure carries moral weight.
Greek kophos (G2974) — blunt, dull of hearing or speech; the crowd's verdict on Christ's ministry in Mar 7:37.
usage: “Thou shalt not curse the deaf… but shalt fear thy God” — cruelty restrained by God alone.
“Who is blind, but my servant? or deaf, as my messenger?” — the charge aimed at the confident.
“He maketh both the deaf to hear, and the dumb to speak” — the promise recorded as done.

pos: n. (the opening of the nose; rendering Hebrew aph, nechiyr)
etymology: From Anglo-Saxon nosthyrl, literally nose-thirl, a nose-hole. The Hebrew aph means both nostril and anger, since the flaring nose was the face of wrath.
biblical_def: Nostril is where Scripture locates the gift and the fragility of life. Man is not made a living soul by his form but by a breath: “the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul” (Gen 2:7). The flood reverses it exactly — “All in whose nostrils was the breath of life… died” (Gen 7:22). Job, in the middle of his misery, still reckons his life a loan held there: “All the while my breath is in me, and the spirit of God is in my nostrils” (Job 27:3). The same word carries the anthropomorphic language of divine wrath — “with the blast of thy nostrils the waters were gathered together” (Exo 15:8) — where the sea itself is parted by what Scripture pictures as God's breath. Nothing in man is more ordinary than breathing, and Scripture makes it the thinnest possible margin between dust and a living soul.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the nostril as an aperture of the nose, the passage through which air is inspired and expired — noting that in Scripture the breath of the nostrils denotes life itself.
webster_full: NOS´TRIL, n. An aperture or opening in the nose; a passage through which air is inspired and expired.
The nostrils are the organs of smelling, and the passages of respiration.
The LORD God breathed into his nostrils the breath of life. Gen. ii.
scriptures: Gen 2:7
And the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.
Job 27:3
All the while my breath is in me, and the spirit of God is in my nostrils;
Exo 15:8
And with the blast of thy nostrils the waters were gathered together, the floods stood upright as an heap, and the depths were congealed in the heart of the sea.
Gen 7:22
All in whose nostrils was the breath of life, of all that was in the dry land, died.
corruption_summary: Man reduced to his chemistry, so that life is an emergent property rather than a breath given — and, correspondingly, treated as disposable at both ends when its usefulness is doubted.
corruption_paragraphs: Genesis 2:7 sets two claims against every materialist account of man. First, the body is genuinely dust — Scripture concedes the chemistry entirely and is never embarrassed by it. Second, the dust does not become a living soul by any arrangement of itself, but by a breath from outside. Remove the second claim and man is a mechanism, and the value of any particular mechanism becomes a matter of function. That is not a slippery slope but a syllogism, and it is worked out at the beginning and the end of every human life.

Job 27:3 gives the pastoral form of the doctrine. In the worst affliction recorded in Scripture, Job does not claim ownership of his life; he says the spirit of God is in his nostrils — borrowed, sustained, and not his to end. A believer who has grasped that his next breath is a loan will hold both his own life and his neighbour's as something belonging to Another, which is finally the only stable ground for the sixth commandment.
roots_summary: Hebrew aph (H639), nostril, nose, and by extension anger — the flaring nostril as the face of wrath; neshamah (H5397), the breath of life God breathed into them.
roots_lines: Hebrew aph (H639) — nostril, nose, face, anger; the same word gives slow to anger, literally long of nostril (Exo 34:6).
Hebrew neshamah (H5397) — breath, spirit; what God breathed into the nostrils, distinguishing man from the beasts formed of the same dust (Gen 2:7).
Hebrew ruach (H7307) — spirit, wind, breath; the spirit of God in Job's nostrils (Job 27:3), sustaining a life he does not own.
usage: “Breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul” — dust plus a breath.
“The spirit of God is in my nostrils” — Job holds his life as a loan.
“With the blast of thy nostrils the waters were gathered together” — the sea parted by breath.

pos: n. (the act of being born; also lineage; rendering Hebrew moledeth, mishbar, Greek genesis, gennao)
etymology: From Old Norse byrdh, related to bear. Scripture uses birth for origin, for lineage, and — decisively — for the second and greater beginning.
biblical_def: Birth in Scripture carries three loads. It is lineage, and lineage does not save: Ezekiel tells Jerusalem, “Thy birth and thy nativity is of the land of Canaan; thy father was an Amorite, and thy mother an Hittite” (Eze 16:3), demolishing every claim of descent. It is the image of a crisis that has come to its extremity: Hezekiah's messengers report, “the children are come to the birth, and there is not strength to bring forth” (Isa 37:3) — the perfect picture of a nation at the point of deliverance with no power to deliver itself, which is exactly when the LORD acts. Ecclesiastes then sets birth beneath death for a man rightly related to God: “A good name is better than precious ointment; and the day of death than the day of one's birth” (Ecc 7:1). And the Lord Jesus makes the whole subject turn on a second one: “Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God” (John 3:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines birth as the act of coming into life, or of being born, and also as lineage, extraction, or descent from parents — and notes the Scriptural sense of the new birth.
webster_full: BIRTH, n. The act of coming into life, or of being born. It is generally applied to human beings.
2. Lineage; extraction; descent; as, Grecian birth.
3. The condition in which a person is born.
4. That which is born; that which is produced, whether animal or vegetable. 5. In Scripture, regeneration is called the new birth.
scriptures: John 3:3
Jesus answered and said unto him, Verily, verily, I say unto thee, Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.
Eze 16:3
And say, Thus saith the Lord GOD unto Jerusalem; Thy birth and thy nativity is of the land of Canaan; thy father was an Amorite, and thy mother an Hittite.
Isa 37:3
And they said unto him, Thus saith Hezekiah, This day is a day of trouble, and of rebuke, and of blasphemy: for the children are come to the birth, and there is not strength to bring forth.
Ecc 7:1
A good name is better than precious ointment; and the day of death than the day of one's birth.
corruption_summary: Birth treated as identity and destiny — a man defined and either credited or condemned by his origin — which is exactly the claim regeneration overturns.
corruption_paragraphs: Every age finds a way to make birth decisive. The ancient version was bloodline and nation; the modern version assigns standing by inherited category and treats it as fixed. Ezekiel 16:3 is the demolition of both: Jerusalem's birth was Canaanite, Amorite, Hittite — and it is this people God takes, washes, and covenants with. Descent settles nothing before God, for credit or for blame.

The gospel's answer is not that birth is unimportant but that a second one is available. John 3:3 makes it the entry requirement of the kingdom, and it is a birth in the strict sense — something done to a person, not by him, since no one contributes to his own conception. That is why regeneration is monergistic and why it cancels the tyranny of origins. And Isaiah 37:3 supplies the pastoral note: the moment of no strength to bring forth is not the end of the story but the point at which God acts.
roots_summary: Hebrew moledeth (H4138), kindred, nativity, birth; mishbar (H4866), the place of breaking forth — the birth-stool of Isa 37:3; Greek gennao (G1080), to beget — born again in John 3:3.
roots_lines: Hebrew moledeth (H4138) — nativity, kindred, birth; Jerusalem's Canaanite origin (Eze 16:3) and Abram's country and kindred he was told to leave.
Hebrew mishbar (H4866) — the breaking-forth place, the mouth of the womb; the children come to the birth with no strength (Isa 37:3).
Greek gennao anothen (G1080, G509) — to be born again, or born from above; both senses are present, and Nicodemus hears only the first (John 3:4).
usage: “Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God” — the kingdom's entry requirement.
“Thy father was an Amorite, and thy mother an Hittite” — descent settles nothing.
“Come to the birth, and there is not strength to bring forth” — and then the LORD acts.

pos: adj. (stained with blood, guilty of bloodshed; rendering Hebrew dam in construct, ish damim)
etymology: From blood, Anglo-Saxon blod. The Hebrew idiom is man of bloods — the plural marking not one killing but a character formed by them.
biblical_def: Bloody in the Authorized Version is a moral verdict, not a description of a stain. The Hebrew phrase behind it is man of bloods, and the psalmist prays plainly, “the LORD will abhor the bloody and deceitful man” (Psa 5:6) — bloodiness and deceit paired, as they were in the devil who was a murderer and a liar from the beginning. David asks not to be gathered with them (Psa 26:9), and warns that “bloody and deceitful men shall not live out half their days” (Psa 55:23). The word cuts close: Shimei hurls it at David himself — “Come out, come out, thou bloody man” (2Sa 16:7) — and David does not answer the charge, because it was not wholly false. The strangest use is Zipporah's at the inn, casting the foreskin at Moses' feet: “Surely a bloody husband art thou to me” (Exo 4:25) — a covenant kept by blood at the last possible moment, and Moses' life spared by it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines bloody as stained with blood, and then as cruel, murderous, given to the shedding of blood, or having a cruel savage disposition.
webster_full: BLOOD´Y, a. Stained with blood; as a bloody garment.
2. Cruel; murderous; given to the shedding of blood; or having a cruel savage disposition; applied to animals.
3. Attended with bloodshed; marked by cruelty; as a bloody battle.
Bloody-minded, having a cruel, ferocious disposition; barbarous.
scriptures: Psa 5:6
Thou shalt destroy them that speak leasing: the LORD will abhor the bloody and deceitful man.
But thou, O God, shalt bring them down into the pit of destruction: bloody and deceitful men shall not live out half their days; but I will trust in thee.
And thus said Shimei when he cursed, Come out, come out, thou bloody man, and thou man of Belial:
Exo 4:25
Then Zipporah took a sharp stone, and cut off the foreskin of her son, and cast it at his feet, and said, Surely a bloody husband art thou to me.
corruption_summary: Bloodshed made entertainment and abstracted by distance, while the church grows squeamish about the blood Scripture insists upon — a culture at ease with violence and uneasy with atonement.
corruption_paragraphs: The inversion is precise and worth naming. Simulated bloodshed is consumed for pleasure at a scale no previous age could have imagined, and real bloodshed is rendered tolerable by distance and euphemism. Meanwhile the same culture — and much of the church with it — finds the blood of the cross distasteful, and hymnody about a fountain filled with blood is quietly retired as primitive. Scripture holds the exact opposite valuation: bloodshed by man is abhorred, and blood shed by God's appointment is the only thing that cleanses.

Exodus 4:25 is the passage that keeps this entry from becoming abstract. On the way to deliver Israel, Moses is met by God and nearly killed over an uncircumcised son, and Zipporah saves him with a flint and a word: a bloody husband art thou to me. It is a scene that resists sentimentality about covenant. God is in earnest about the sign He appointed, and the deliverer of Israel is not exempt from it. Blood was required then, and blood is required still — which is why the gospel is not squeamish.
roots_summary: Hebrew dam (H1818), blood; the idiom ish damim, a man of bloods, marking a settled character; chatan damim (Exo 4:25), a bridegroom or husband of blood.
roots_lines: Hebrew dam (H1818) — blood; in the plural damim it denotes bloodguilt, the blood that cries from the ground (Gen 4:10).
Hebrew ish damim — a man of bloods; the abhorred figure of Psa 5:6 and Psa 55:23, and Shimei's charge against David (2Sa 16:7).
Hebrew chatan damim — a husband of blood; Zipporah's startling phrase at the inn, tying marriage, covenant, and circumcision together (Exo 4:25).
usage: “The LORD will abhor the bloody and deceitful man” — bloodshed and lying always travel together.
“Come out, come out, thou bloody man” — and David did not answer it.
“Surely a bloody husband art thou to me” — the covenant kept at the last moment.

pos: v. (to wash the body in water, especially for ceremonial cleansing; rendering Hebrew rachats)
etymology: From Anglo-Saxon bathian. In Leviticus the word is technical: not hygiene but the appointed removal of ceremonial uncleanness.
biblical_def: Bathe in the Authorized Version belongs almost entirely to the law of cleansing, and Leviticus 15 repeats it with deliberate monotony: whoever touches the unclean thing “shall wash his clothes, and bathe himself in water, and be unclean until the even” (Lev 15:5, 15:6, 15:7, and on through the chapter). Two features of the formula preach. First, the uncleanness is contagious — it passes by touch, while cleanness does not — which is the whole logic of the ceremonial system and the reason the Lord Jesus touching a leper is so startling a reversal. Second, even after washing, the man remains unclean until the even: cleansing is real but not instantaneous, and a day must pass. For the deeper cleansing the law requires running water: “wash his clothes, and bathe his flesh in running water, and shall be clean” (Lev 15:13) — literally living water, the phrase the Lord Jesus later claims for Himself.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines bathe as to wash the body, or a part of it, by immersion or by applying water — and notes its use for washing for pleasure, for health, or for religious purification.
webster_full: BATHE, v.t. To wash the body, or some part of it, by immersion, as in a bath.
2. To wash or moisten, for the purpose of making soft and supple, or for cleansing.
3. To moisten or suffuse with a liquid; as, to bathe in tears or blood.
BATHE, v.i. To be or lie in a bath; to be in water, or in other liquid.
scriptures: And when he that hath an issue is cleansed of his issue; then he shall number to himself seven days for his cleansing, and wash his clothes, and bathe his flesh in running water, and shall be clean.
Lev 15:5
And whosoever toucheth his bed shall wash his clothes, and bathe himself in water, and be unclean until the even.
And whomsoever he toucheth that hath the issue, and hath not rinsed his hands in water, he shall wash his clothes, and bathe himself in water, and be unclean until the even.
The woman also with whom man shall lie with seed of copulation, they shall both bathe themselves in water, and be unclean until the even.
corruption_summary: The ceremonial law dismissed as primitive taboo, so that the categories it was teaching — that defilement is real, contagious, and needs an appointed remedy — are lost with it.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live error is dismissal: Leviticus 15 is read as ancient hygiene or superstition, and skipped. But the chapter is teaching a doctrine by repetition. Uncleanness spreads by contact and cleanness does not, which trains a people to understand that sin is communicable and holiness is not transferred by proximity. Every reader who has watched one compromised man contaminate a household or a congregation has seen Leviticus 15 confirmed.

The principle to recover is that the whole apparatus is a schoolmaster pointing forward. The requirement of running water in verse 13 — living water, not a standing pool — is not a footnote; it is the vocabulary the Lord Jesus takes up at the well and in the temple courts. And the direction of contagion reverses at His touch: the leper is cleansed rather than the Christ defiled. The bathing of Leviticus was never able to reach further than the skin and until the evening; what it pictured reaches the conscience and forever.
roots_summary: Hebrew rachats (H7364), to wash, bathe — used of the body, while kabas is used of clothes; mayim chayyim, living or running water, required for the fullest cleansing.
roots_lines: Hebrew rachats (H7364) — to wash, bathe the body; the standing requirement of Leviticus 15 and of the priests at the laver.
Hebrew kabas (H3526) — to wash by treading, used of garments; the law distinguishes washing clothes from bathing flesh in the same breath.
Hebrew mayim chayyim (H4325, H2416) — living water, running water; required in Lev 15:13, and claimed by Christ in John 4 and John 7.
usage: “Bathe himself in water, and be unclean until the even” — cleansing real, but not instantaneous.
“Bathe his flesh in running water, and shall be clean” — living water, not a standing pool.
Uncleanness passes by touch and cleanness does not — until Christ touches the leper.

pos: n. and v. (the sense of odour; to perceive by that sense; rendering Hebrew riach, reyach)
etymology: Of uncertain origin, appearing in Middle English. Scripture makes this the most theological of the senses, because it is the sense by which God is said to receive a sacrifice.
biblical_def: Smell is the sense Scripture attaches to acceptance. After the flood, “the LORD smelled a sweet savour” and resolved not to curse the ground again for man's sake (Gen 8:21) — the whole covenant with creation follows a smell rising from an altar. Conversely, judgment is announced as a refusal to smell: “I will not smell the savour of your sweet odours” (Lev 26:31), which is worse than rejection; it is God declining even to receive. The blessing of Jacob turns on the same sense: “he smelled the smell of his raiment, and blessed him, and said, See, the smell of my son is as the smell of a field which the LORD hath blessed” (Gen 27:27) — a son blessed for a fragrance not his own, wearing another's garment, which the Reformed reader will recognize at once. And the psalmist's mockery of idols ends here: “noses have they, but they smell not” (Psa 115:6). The dead gods cannot receive what is offered them.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines smell as the faculty of perceiving by the nose, and the quality of any thing which affects that organ — scent, odour — noting the Scriptural use of a sweet savour for what is acceptable to God.
webster_full: SMELL, v.t. To perceive by the nose; to have a sensation excited by the effluvia of a substance applied to the nose.
SMELL, n. The faculty of perceiving by the nose, or the organs of smell; the sense of smelling.
2. The quality of any thing which affects the olfactory organs; odor; scent; as the smell of mint.
A sweet smell, or savour, in Scripture, denotes that which is acceptable to God.
scriptures: Gen 8:21

And the LORD smelled a sweet savour; and the LORD said in his heart, I will not again curse the ground any more for man's sake; for the imagination of man's heart is evil from his youth; neither will I again smite any more every thing living, as I have done.
And he came near, and kissed him: and he smelled the smell of his raiment, and blessed him, and said, See, the smell of my son is as the smell of a field which the LORD hath blessed:
And I will make your cities waste, and bring your sanctuaries unto desolation, and I will not smell the savour of your sweet odours.
They have ears, but they hear not: noses have they, but they smell not:
corruption_summary: Worship judged by what it does to the worshipper rather than by whether God receives it — the one question Leviticus 26:31 makes decisive.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The drift is in worship, and it is a drift of direction. Where a service is evaluated by the congregation's experience of it, the whole biblical question has been reversed. Scripture's test is whether the LORD smells a sweet savour — whether the offering is received — and Leviticus 26:31 shows the terrifying alternative: not lightning, but a God who simply does not inhale. Worship can be sincere, well-attended, and unsmelled.

Genesis 27:27 is the passage to recover, and the Reformed reader will see the doctrine at once. Jacob receives the blessing while wearing his brother's garments, and it is the smell of the raiment that draws the blessing down: the smell of my son is as the smell of a field which the LORD hath blessed. The deception was Jacob's sin and God's election stood regardless; but the picture is imputed righteousness in miniature — a man accepted in a garment not his own, smelled and blessed for a fragrance he did not produce.
roots_summary: Hebrew riach (H7306), to smell, perceive odour; reyach (H7381), a savour, odour; reyach nichoach, a sweet or restful savour — the technical phrase for an accepted offering.
roots_lines: Hebrew riach (H7306) — to smell; used of the LORD receiving Noah's offering (Gen 8:21) and of Isaac blessing Jacob (Gen 27:27).
Hebrew reyach nichoach (H7381, H5207) — a savour of rest, a sweet savour; the standing formula for a sacrifice God accepts (Exo 29:18).
Greek euodia (G2175) — a sweet smell; Paul applies it to Christ's offering (Eph 5:2) and to the gifts of the Philippians (Php 4:18).
usage: “The LORD smelled a sweet savour” — a covenant with creation follows a smell from an altar.
“I will not smell the savour of your sweet odours” — worse than rejection.
“The smell of my son is as the smell of a field which the LORD hath blessed” — blessed in another's garment.
